question: Which statement best describes The internal [[Prototype]] slot?
options: Every object has a hidden internal slot called [[Prototype]] that points to another object (or null). This is the link the engine follows during property lookup. You can read it with Object.getPrototypeOf(obj) and the legacy accessor __proto__, but the slot itself is internal machinery, not a normal property.

These two are constantly confused. `prototype` is a property that exists ONLY on functions — it's the object that will become the [[Prototype]] of instances created with `new`. `__proto__` is an accessor present on objects that exposes their own [[Prototype]] link. In short: functions have `prototype`, instances have `__proto__`, and `instance.__proto__ === Constructor.prototype`.

Reading obj.x checks obj's own properties first. If not found, the engine looks at obj's [[Prototype]], then that object's [[Prototype]], and so on up the chain. The first match wins; if nothing matches, the result is undefined. Writing obj.x = v, by contrast, sets an OWN property on obj rather than modifying the prototype.

Objects link to their prototype, which links to its prototype, forming a chain that ends at Object.prototype and finally null. This chain is what the engine traverses to resolve properties and methods, giving JavaScript its inheritance without copying anything.

question: Which statement best describes Constructor functions?
options: Classical languages (Java, C++) copy structure from classes into instances at instantiation. JavaScript is prototypal: objects delegate to other live objects at lookup time. `class` syntax looks classical but is pure sugar over prototypes — there are no real classes underneath, only objects linked to prototypes.
